sentences.label: Lowering the risk
sentences.text: These add up independently, and these lower the risk: compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 29% to about 3%, non-anginal chest pain to about 5% and atypical angina to about 14%; being a woman lowers it to about 3% and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 14%; and through this sum alone a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 32% at 118 to about 28% at 175 beats per minute (maximum heart rate also acts through the age and heart rate gate, below).

sentences.label: Raising the risk
sentences.text: Each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same, from about 29% at 0 to about 94% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher; higher resting blood pressure raises it steadily, from about 20% at 110 mm Hg to about 44% at 155 mm Hg, and chest pain brought on by exercise raises it to about 43%.

Through this sum alone, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 73%, higher cholesterol raises it steadily from about 18% at 193 mg/dL to about 49% at 308 mg/dL, and a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises it to about 42%; all three also act through the parts below.

sentences.label: Rare results
sentences.text: Some rarer results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 2 to 17): through this sum alone a downsloping ST segment raises the risk to about 50% and a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 11%, and an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG raises it to about 46%.

This part reads age, maximum heart rate and the thallium scan, and acts on 80 of 242 training patients, 9 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 4% without it and about 1% with it.

For patients without a reversible defect on the thallium scan, it switches on when age in years minus about 0.28 × the maximum heart rate in beats per minute is below about 11.4 (for maximum heart rates from about 71 to 202 beats per minute); 80 of 242 training patients are on that side, and 11% of them had heart disease, against 60% of the others.

Through it, older age raises the predicted risk steadily up to about 56 years (between 45 and 61 years for different patients), then no further for most patients, but for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it rises in a jump: for a typical patient from about 12% at 42 to about 29% at 66 years.

Across the whole model, a higher maximum heart rate lowers the risk in an uneven way, more without a reversible defect on the thallium scan (from about 32% at 118 to about 21% at 175 beats per minute, against about 45% to about 40% with one).

This part reads only ST depression on exercise and acts on 121 of 242 training patients, 77 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 89% without it and about 91% with it.

Through it, more ST depression raises the predicted risk slowly at first, then faster, adding risk only once it rises above about 0.8 mm: for a typical patient from about 29% at 0 mm to about 48% at 2.8 mm.

This part reads the slope of the ST segment, ST depression on exercise and cholesterol, and acts on 117 of 242 training patients, 78 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 86% without it and about 90% with it.

For patients whose ST segment is not flat, it switches on when ST depression on exercise is above about 2.23 mm (for cholesterol from about 126 to 186 mg/dL), or when ST depression minus about 0.012 × the cholesterol in mg/dL is above about 0.011 (for cholesterol from about 186 to 417 mg/dL); 117 of 242 training patients are on, and 67% of them had heart disease, against 23% of the others.

Across the whole model, more ST depression raises the risk slowly at first, then faster, and even more so with a flat ST segment: from about 75% to about 91% then, against about 29% to about 48% otherwise.

Higher cholesterol raises it steadily across the whole model, from about 67% to about 88% with a flat ST segment and from about 18% to about 49% otherwise, while through this part it lowers the risk in an uneven way, for the typical patient the part acts on from about 91% to about 88%.

lead.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results) the model predicts a risk of heart disease of about 29%; it adds up most of its inputs independently, and three parts add to that sum: one acts on 80 of 242 training patients through age and maximum heart rate, one on 121 through ST depression on exercise, and one on 117 through the ST segment, ST depression and cholesterol.

evidence.text: For patients without a reversible defect on the thallium scan, it switches on when age in years minus about 0.28 × the maximum heart rate in beats per minute is below about 11.4 (for maximum heart rates from about 71 to 202 beats per minute); 80 of 242 training patients are on that side, and 11% of them had heart disease, against 60% of the others.

Through it, older age raises the predicted risk steadily up to about 56 years (between 45 and 61 years for different patients), then no further for most patients, but for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it rises in a jump: for a typical patient from about 12% at 42 to about 29% at 66 years.
Across the whole model, older age raises the risk, then no further, only if the thallium scan shows no reversible defect: from about 12% to about 29%, while with one it stays at about 42%.

A higher maximum heart rate lowers the risk through it in an uneven way, from about 29% at 118 to about 22% at 175 beats per minute, and across the whole model it lowers it more without a reversible defect (from about 32% to about 21%, against about 45% to about 40%).
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 242 training patients.

hypothesis.text: This part lowers the predicted risk for patients whose age is low relative to their maximum heart rate; for the typical patient it acts on, a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises the risk through it from about 1% to about 4%.

evidence.text: It acts on 117 of 242 training patients, 78 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 86% without it and about 90% with it.

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 77%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 29%) (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 73%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 29%) (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, ST depression on exercise only adds to the predicted risk of heart disease once it rises above about 0.8 mm: for a typical such patient, going from 0.0 mm to 3.5 mm moves it from about 29% to about 57% (on the training data only).

A higher age clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, but only if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan (steadily up to about 54 years, then no further for patients with thallium stress test result other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan): for a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 12% to about 29% if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan, and from about 42% to about 42% if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect.

analysis.note: Ablations remove a child's readout from the logit (zero and mean ablation give the same AUC because readouts enter additively). Linear replacement = least-squares refit of the child's logit contribution on its own raw inputs. The nonlinear block adds +0.013 train AUC over the linear core; the heart-rate-reserve gate carries most of it (0.006).

record.summary: Mostly logistic regression: 16 direct edges (logit SD 3.24; train AUC 0.930 alone) plus three additive nonlinear corrections (logit SD 0.95) to 0.943. Largest: a protective heart-rate-reserve gate ReLU(-1.52 - 1.50 age + 1.02 thalach - 1.56 thal:7) read out -0.61, open for half the patients without a reversible defect; then a flat-ST-slope gate scaled by oldpeak and down by cholesterol, and a convex two-kink oldpeak dose-response. Age and oldpeak act only through these gates. Same mechanisms as the generation-38 heart-s2 record, weights shifted by at most about 0.03 after retraining.
